title: Conseil constitutionnel censures surveillance loi, citing libertés fondamentales
content: The Conseil constitutionnel censured two central articles of the loi sur la surveillance numérique on Tuesday evening, ruling that the bulk retention of connection data for twenty-four months was disproportionate and infringed the libertés fondamentales protected by the Union Charter.

The decision, adopted by seven votes to four, strikes down the provision that allowed the intelligence services to collect metadata without prior authorisation from an independent commission, and a second article that extended such collection to municipal networks. The remainder of the law, including the framework for targeted interception, survives.

The challenge had been brought through a *référé* by the barreau d’Aurelle, joined by three digital-rights organisations and a group of academics. “The court has restored a principle that parliaments tend to forget: capability is not authorisation,” said Maître Odile Fargeon, who led the case.

The Ministry of the Interior said it would study the decision before adjusting the implementation *décret*. Paul Grandet, the minister, had defended the law as an “ordinary instrument of a modern state” during the hearings, and police syndicats warned on Wednesday that the censure would interrupt several ongoing investigations into organised fraud.

Legal scholars noted that the reasoning relies on the same proportionality test the Conseil used in 2021 to uphold the earlier surveillance framework, and that the difference now lies in the scale of retention. “The court has not changed its doctrine; the technology changed the facts,” said Professor Léa Santerre of the Université d’Aurelle.

The government has announced that a replacement bill will be prepared for the spring session. Whether it can secure a majority is uncertain: the censure was welcomed by parts of the governing coalition, and two ministers have publicly argued that the intelligence services should now seek warrants on an individual basis.
author: Agence des Républiques (ADR)
